articles.title_orig: One photo that captures the historic talks between China, US and Russia
articles.title_zh: One photo that captures the historic talks between China, US and Russia
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

articles.title_orig: Stocks slide despite Anthropic’s record debut and Trump touts ‘unbelievable’ China summit: Morning Rundown
articles.title_zh: Stocks slide despite Anthropic’s record debut and Trump touts ‘unbelievable’ China summit: Morning Rundown
articles.content_orig:
Morning Rundown: Deadly Russian strikes hit 3 Kyiv bridges, huge storms slam East and West coasts, and Google faces backlash over AI in schools
Stocks fell despite Anthropic’s record-setting public debut. Trump calls his meetings with Xi and Putin “amazing.” And why Google is getting backlash from some of the nation’s largest school districts.
Here’s what to know today.
Anthropic, the AI giant behind Claude, shattered the record for the largest-ever public offering, raising at least $81 billion and closing at $97 a share in its market debut, valuing the company at more than $1.7 trillion. It surpassed SpaceX, which raised $75 billion in June.
This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox.
But the blockbuster debut wasn’t enough to calm broader concerns about AI and tech, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite falling more than 2% by Thursday’s close.
Heavy borrowing, rising computing costs and uncertainty over the future of data centers following Democratic election victories have begun to weigh on the AI investment boom. And that was before the Jensen Huang scandal cast a cloud over Nvidia.
Some experts say Anthropic’s IPO was exactly what the industry needed to “revive overall sentiment,” a wealth management executive said.
What analysts make of Anthropic’s IPO.
President Donald Trump may be facing low approval ratings and a resurgent Democratic opposition at home, but in China he received a very different reception.
“It was unbelievable,” Trump told NBC News in a phone call. “They treated me as well as a person could be treated.”
Chinese President Xi Jinping broke precedent to greet Trump on the tarmac and later gave him a red-carpet sendoff. And despite disdain for Vladimir Putin among some U.S. lawmakers, Trump called the Russian president his “friend.”
Trump rated the summit, which featured historic trilateral talks with Putin and Xi and separate meetings with both leaders, “on a scale of zero to 10 … a 12,” calling the talks “just amazing, amazing meetings.”
Whether that warmth translates into peace deals in Iran or Ukraine, however, remains far from clear. Trump said he agreed with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy that any deal negotiated by Trump, Putin and Xi would not succeed without Kyiv’s approval.
Hours after the summit, Russia launched a massive ballistic missile attack on Kyiv , striking three bridges, Ukrainian officials said, following Putin’s vow of “painful” retaliation for attacks on Russia’s prized Crimea Bridge.
Read the full analysis here.
Elon Musk declared he’s not MAGA. Palantir CEO Alex Karp, who once described his company as anti-woke, now touts his left-wing credentials. Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos says he’s worked with every president since the 1990s — not just Trump.
Trump yesterday responded to Musk’s comments in a phone call with NBC News , saying that when people “veer” from MAGA, “they don’t do very well.”
None of the company leaders have directly criticized the president, but their comments suggest some are recalibrating their public posture as Democrats plot a path back to the White House. But don’t expect to see a dramatic swing toward the left, a tech insider said. “Trump is still there, and he still keeps score.”
How the CEOs’ rhetoric has shifted since the midterms.
Storms have battered both the East and West coasts this week as El Niño, the climate pattern that intensifies Pacific weather systems and brings increased rainfall to the Southeast, reaches record levels.
Downtown San Francisco saw 2.64 inches of rain on Wednesday, breaking a daily rainfall record set in 1918. In the Bay Area and further south in Santa Cruz, two waterspouts formed. Elsewhere, gusty winds downed trees and power lines and set off flash flood warnings.
In the Southeast, parts of Florida saw more than a foot of rain fall in a single day . Preliminary figures showed 15.3 inches of rain in parts of Broward County, the National Weather Service said. Flood threats continued today along the Atlantic coast. The same areas were battered with historic rainfall just two weeks ago.
Read more about this week’s weather.
When I’ve asked educators why they trust Google, they usually say it’s because the tech giant listens to them. I spoke to former company leaders who said its education products were developed after employees spent time in classrooms with teachers. And that’s why they say that Google’s decision to let schools turn off Search entirely — but not disable the AI Overview on search results — evoked such a backlash.
Now leaders of the largest school districts — New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago — are considering switching every student laptop so that they don’t use Google Search. Ex-Googlers are also speaking out against the current approach on generative AI’s incorporation into software used by schools.
Google has stood firm so far, saying they are trying to give schools more control, not less. I wrote about why this has become such a flashpoint , how the company became so important to classrooms and what schools are doing to limit its influence. — Tyler Kingkade , enterprise reporter
Holiday prep is officially underway. From the best artificial Christmas trees to gifts that’ll give your friends and family a well-deserved break , our NBC Selected shopping editors pulled together the essentials for a cozier season. They also rounded up the best beauty advent calendars to count down the holidays and the 100 best gifts for everyone on your list.
Sign up to The Selection newsletter for hands-on product reviews, expert shopping tips and a look at the best deals and sales each week.
Thanks for reading today’s Morning Rundown. Today’s newsletter was curated for you by Elizabeth Robinson and Josephine Murphy. If you’re a fan, please send a link to your family and friends. They can sign up here .
Elizabeth Robinson is a newsletter editor for NBC News, based in Los Angeles.
Josephine Murphy is an NBC News platforms intern based in Los Angeles.

articles.title_orig: Poland condemns Russian 'provocation' after three airspace violations
articles.title_zh: Poland condemns Russian 'provocation' after three airspace violations
articles.content_orig:
Russian missile crash in Poland likely an intentional provocation as European militaries hold drills, Polish leader says
WARSAW, Poland -- Russian missile crash in Poland likely an intentional provocation as European militaries hold drills, Polish leader says.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below.
The Polish military is investigating a “suspected violation” of the country's airspace near its border with Ukraine after officials sought to retrieve an unidentified object that had apparently crash-landed in Poland on Friday morning.
The incident came against the backdrop of Russian attacks in Ukraine that killed three people, injured nine others and damaged bridges and transport infrastructure. Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said he believes the incident was another provocation by Russia and timed to European military exercises underway in Poland.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he would convene a meeting with government ministers, military commanders and the head of security services in response. Officials said it was too early to tell what the object was.
The potential crash site is near the village of Nowy Lipowiec, roughly 60 kilometers (37 miles) from the Poland-Ukraine border. Nearby schools suspended classes for the day, according to Polish news agency PAP.
Images from closed-circuit cameras and a mobile phone in the region collected by PAP showed a large, loud explosion in a bright flash that appeared to take place in a wooded area.
Military helicopters and rescue vehicles were spotted in the vicinity, and police set up temporary roadblocks as an investigation was underway.
The location is also about 75 kilometers (47 miles) from where thousands of European troops were taking part on Friday in an unprecedented military exercise in southeastern Poland to prepare for a potential postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilize the country and rebuild its military once the war ends.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Anthropic Stock Drops Premarket as Tech Rout Intensifies
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Anthropic Stock Drops Premarket as Tech Rout Intensifies
articles.content_orig:
Asian markets on track for their worst week since 2020, with European and US stocks also way down
Business live – latest updates
Global stock markets have slumped as Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.
Asian stock markets were on track for their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell on Friday. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.
The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.
In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets were heading for their worst week since March, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.3% in the first 90 minutes.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO .
Anthropic’s shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the frontier AI firm began. But they were heading for losses on Friday, down 6% at $91.30, falling back towards the IPO price of $83.
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.
“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.
Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI build out.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.
after newsletter promotion
“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index hit a five-month low on Friday morning. It has dropped by 4.8% this week, and is heading for its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.
Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.

Nato scrambled jets on Friday after Poland said its airspace had been violated several times during a Russian attack on Ukraine.
Military aircraft were operating in Polish airspace while ground-based air defences were made ready , the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces said in a statement.
“These actions are preventive in nature and are aimed at securing and protecting Polish airspace, especially in areas adjacent to those under threat,” it added.
Poland earlier reported that three objects crossed over from Russia, likely including a KH-101 cruise missile, another missile and a drone.
Defence minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz condemned what he called a “provocation” from Moscow and said he would ask Nato for additional support on its eastern flank.
He assessed that it was unlikely to be a coincidence, occurring as Poland was set to hold military exercises of the 'Coalition of the Willing' of Ukraine's allies on Friday.
Russia’s foreign ministry says it will take ‘necessary measures’ after Estonia said it was closing its border with Russia.
The Baltic country's government said on Friday it would close its road border crossings with Russia on security grounds from December 1 and will decide after six months whether to extend the suspension.
Estonia on Sunday accused Russian security services of staging an attempted arson attack on an Estonian defence company, in what it said was the second such incident this year.
Estonia's northern neighbour Finland shut its Russia border crossings in 2023, and has kept them closed since then, while southern Baltic nations Latvia and Lithuania maintain open crossings.
Polish prime minister Donald Tusk said on Friday that the incursions into Polish airspace do not look like an accident but an “intentional provocation” from Russia.
"We know that what landed on Polish soil came from Russia,” he claimed in a press conference.
“Therefore — and this is not just my own assessment, but also that of our foreign partners, including those within NATO — it does not look like an accident. It appears that we are dealing with an intentional provocation.”
This week repeated Ukrainian strikes have seriously damaged the 19km (12-mile) Crimean Bridge, which straddles the Kerch Strait that links the Black and Azov seas.
The span is vital to sustaining Russia’s military operations, and the £3bn bridge is a potent reminder of Russia’s illegal annexation of the Crimean Peninsula, making it a prime target for Ukraine.
Train traffic stopped after the latest overnight strike into Thursday while authorities assessed the damage, but it resumed in the afternoon, according to Russian state news agency RIA Novosti.
The Ukrainian strikes seemed calculated to embarrass Putin as he met in China with Xi and Trump, as well as to undermine Russia's argument that its victory is inevitable.
In China, Putin insisted the bridge is a civilian asset, adding that he had ordered it closed to carrying military hardware or ammunition.
Putin also said that the road side of the bridge had been “seriously damaged” but vowed to rebuild it. The rail section, which runs parallel to the road, is believed to be stronger in order to bear the greater weight of cargo transport.
Ukraine’s defense ministry said the successful operation to target the bridge meant Russia would need to reroute fuel and ammunition supplies over land, where “our drones are waiting for the cargo.”
The US president should be embarrassed to be rubbing shoulders in this ‘fraternity of autocrats’ with a Russian leader wanted for war crimes by the ICC – but has shown he will stop at nothing for a seat with the ‘big men’ at the table, says Sam Kiley
In China, Trump called Putin “my friend.” The American president’s relationship with Zelensky has soured recently, although the question of US support for Ukraine could be raised by Democrats who will take control of Congress in January after their wins in the midterm elections.
European leaders have tried to isolate Putin diplomatically and have heavily sanctioned the Russian economy as they fear being sidelined by Trump’s direct talks with Putin.
Kushner said that, in his talks with Putin and Xi, Trump “sent a very strong message to both of them on the desire for peace and would like to engage both of them very aggressively to get there.”
He deferred to Trump on giving any details of the “private discussions,” but added: “I believe he also came away believing that peace is achievable and we need to all work together to try and achieve it.”
Putin said in Shenzhen that the Kremlin is not against European participation in talks, but “we need to understand with what Europe will come to these negotiations.” The Kremlin has proposed to European officials through diplomatic channels to come to Moscow “to determine their position,” Putin said, without elaborating. No date has been set.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov declined to say which European officials had been invited or whether Moscow had received a response, Russian state news agency Tass reported.
Polish authorities were investigating reports that at least two unknown objects had come down near the border with Ukraine after the army said Polish airspace might have been violated during Russian strikes on Ukraine.
Authorities in Nato-member Poland said it was too early to say what the objects were. A Ukrainian air force spokesperson said it was likely that a Russian missile had crossed into Poland.
The Russian embassy in Warsaw did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.
Drones have repeatedly strayed into the airspace of countries on Nato’s eastern flank since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, fuelling tension ⁠with the military alliance and stoking fears that the war could spread.
"We confirm the crash of an unidentified object in the village of Nowy Lipowiec," the district prosecutor's office in Lublin wrote on X. "Reports regarding potential additional objects in the region are currently being verified by the relevant services."
Footage shared on ‌social media from what appeared to be a security camera at a property in the nearby village of Chmielek showed an explosion in the distance.
Polish infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak said on X that a traffic controller had heard a loud bang near railway premises in Rudnik nad Sanem, about 50km west of Nowy Lipowiec. He said no visible damage to the railway had been found but that an inspection vehicle had been dispatched.
Klimczak also said air traffic controllers had been evacuated at the airport in Rzeszow, the largest city in southeastern Poland.
Prime minister Donald Tusk said he had received reports about security in ​the area and that there was currently no threat from the ‌air.
President Karol Nawrocki was ⁠also informed about the situation.
Vladimir Putin was given a warm reception during the trilateral summit with Trump and Xi. The latest casualty figures are a stark reminder of the devastation the Russian leader has brought to Ukraine, writes James C. Reynolds:
Russian deputy foreign minister ​Sergei Ryabkov on Friday pushed back against the idea of Nato-style security guarantees for Ukraine and said what he called any form of "quasi membership" for Kyiv of the Western military alliance ⁠was totally unacceptable for Moscow, Russian state media reported.
Ryabkov made the comments a day after French president Emmanuel Macron said after a Berlin summit that the question of Ukraine's Nato membership should be reopened. US envoy Jared Kushner said at the same event that he and fellow negotiator Steve Witkoff had "gotten the Russians comfortable with the concept that any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5”. articles.title_orig: The UK and EU hold a rare summit to strengthen ties as Burnham seeks to mend Brexit damage
articles.title_zh: The UK and EU hold a rare summit to strengthen ties as Burnham seeks to mend Brexit damage
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences, and just perhaps, to pave the way for them to get back together.
Burnham is scheduled to hold just under an hour of talks in Brussels with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen . Then they'll all meet in a plenary session with U.K. government ministers and European commissioners.
Burnham has described the rare EU-U.K. summit — only the second since Britain became the first country to leave the world’s biggest trading bloc — as a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce.
“The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained,” he said this week.
Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc. But he's stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining.
Ahead of the meeting, von der Leyen said she wanted it to be “a summit of ambition and concrete results. More opportunities for young people. Easier agrifood trade. And a stronger cooperation on economic security.”
The two sides are expected to sign a trade deal for food and drink, an agreement on emissions trading and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU. Burnham says the deals could add a modest 0.4% to Britain’s economy.
The war in Ukraine, and the U.K.’s military strength, are drawing the two back together, and the summit provides the EU with an opportunity to discuss stronger cooperation on security and defense, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration.
“Our security and prosperity are closely intertwined, making a strong partnership between us essential,” Costa said ahead of the meeting. “By deepening our cooperation, we can strengthen our ability to address the challenges of our time, strengthen our resilience and promote stability in Europe and beyond.”
Nevertheless, feelings remain raw, and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the U.K. rejoining. They are weary from the shifting demands of seven British prime ministers over the last decade and want real clarity about the country’s intentions.
Ireland’s ambassador in London, Sonja Hyland, said that when Britain voted for Brexit, “there was a lack of clarity as to exactly what that meant.” If Britain wants to reopen negotiations, she said, it must “make a clear decision as to what it wants.”
Lawless reported from London.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic's $1.5 trillion IPO sets off a fresh wave of tech wealth heading for South Florida
articles.title_zh: Anthropic's $1.5 trillion IPO sets off a fresh wave of tech wealth heading for South Florida
articles.content_orig:
BH Group’s Isaac Toledano and West Palm Beach developer Kenneth Baboun speak to Fox News Digital about a tech exodus hitting Florida after Anthropic’s record-setting IPO debut.
Now live on the Nasdaq, Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion stock market debut is poised to mint a fresh class of overnight multimillionaires. While Wall Street cheers one of the largest public listings in history, real estate and finance insiders say South Florida is nearing an irreversible "point of no return," as newly liquid tech engineers and institutional backers look to escape high-tax states like California and New York for the Sunshine State’s booming business corridor.
Buying a piece of the IPO action themselves, BH Group CEO Isaac Toledano and West Palm Beach developer and former financial executive Kenneth Baboun are predicting a new tech exodus wave ripping through Florida by mid-to-end of 2027.
"I think we're on the verge of it … People do get tired of being abused, if you will, by your government, not letting you work freely and make money. So I think we're very close to reaching that line that will be a point of no return. We're almost there," Baboun told Fox News Digital.
"Nobody can ignore and forget what Ken Griffin said a few years ago that Chicago's streets are not safe anymore," Toledano also told Fox News Digital. "Everybody wants to follow the smart money, and definitely, it looks like the smart money made the decision that, what we see in South Florida, it's real, and it's here to stay."
INSIDE KEN GRIFFIN'S SECRET THREE-YEAR NEGOTIATION FOR FLORIDA'S LARGEST REAL ESTATE DEAL IN HISTORY
The AI giant and Claude maker’s highly anticipated IPO was priced at $83 per share before beginning trading on Thursday. The listing follows SpaceX’s historic market debut in June, and sets up a massive liquidity event for both early institutional backers and rank-and-file AI engineers once post-IPO lockup periods expire.
Newfound Anthropic IPO wealth could be heading to South Florida, real estate insiders tell Fox News Digital. (Getty Images)
Toledano noted that, after SpaceX’s IPO, a friend who netted $188 million immediately called to buy a luxury condo. Now, Toledano said he’s in active negotiations with a California tech billionaire eyeing a $110 million penthouse at BH Group's newly launched Raffles Residences Coconut Grove.
"The idea behind some of these new millionaires and billionaires [is] keeping some of the money either in stocks, or maybe investing some of their money in real estate, which is a real tangible asset. I think that [people still] learn the lesson from the dot-com days and maybe the financial crisis in 2008, and I think that a lot of people will diversify their investments," Toledano explained.
"We still see buyers coming from California, New York, Chicago, a lot of these blue states," he added.
Baboun noted the excitement around new generational wealth for Anthropic’s workforce and for decentralized investors, believing that Florida is "the best place in the U.S. to be living in" and the best target for potential new residents.
Stuart Varney and Charles Payne discuss the massive wealth creation from the Anthropic IPO. Charles Payne defends the capitalist system, explaining how it raises global living standards and changes lives.
"I do not expect any money from Anthropic to be coming here in the next 45 days that we have left of the year. I do believe next year, as they are able to realize gains, people will be doing some type of tax planning to change their tax residency, and Florida has been very friendly to receive them over here," he said. "What we have seen already in the market has been extreme traffic from California, Texas, Georgia, New York … Since we had the midterms and what happened with that, people are looking into Florida more actively."
The developers and Anthropic stock owners also claimed the market is already seeing heavy migration traffic triggered by recent election cycles and high-tax state policies, creating a further pipeline of demand. Baboun offered that 80% of West Palm Beach buyers still hail from New York and Chicago, California traffic has surged — and buyers who once considered Texas are pivoting to Florida to avoid political and regulatory uncertainty.
"We have a very friendly government that you can come and do business. They don't penalize you for doing business like New York does," Baboun said. "It's really like a perfect storm that we've incubated here."
Toledano agreed, spotlighting the contrast between Republican-backed tax cuts in Florida and rising tax burdens in blue states.
Leaders and attendees at The Real Deal Miami Real Estate Forum speak to Fox News Digital about the passing of Florida’s Amendment 3, which expands homestead exemptions on primary residences.
"I think this is the side effect of the results of the election," he said. "I think that Florida, still being a red state, the state is very active on bringing [in] a lot of companies — companies are still relocating here — pushing real estate taxes down, sending a message to people that while other states pushing their taxes and the real estate taxes up, in Florida, we do exactly the opposite."
According to Barron’s, Anthropic’s IPO filing shows employee stock options alone exceed $100 billion even at the bottom of the pricing range, translating to an average windfall of roughly $20 million per worker, though actual payouts vary by rank and tenure. At the very top, the Bloomberg Billionaires Index previously pegged each of the AI giant’s seven co-founders at an estimated $18 billion fortune based on the IPO's earlier pricing range.
Toledano pointed out that when executives move to Florida, they’re often breaking records on $50 million to $80 million estates in Palm Beach , Coral Gables or Fisher Island, while lower-rank employees can fuel demand for $1.5 million to $3 million waterfront condos in Hollywood and Pompano Beach. Baboun made the assessment that South Florida’s massive post-COVID office construction boom also leaves the commercial market ready for incoming AI firms.
"It's exciting to see other people realize their American dream. It's sad that in parts of this great country, you get penalized for doing that."
"Not all their employees can afford to buy $50 to $60 to $80 million homes in Palm Beach or in Coral Gables or in Coconut Grove. So this is why rentals are still going to do [well] here," Toledano said.
"When we had the pressure of the hedge funds coming down, we were not prepared," Baboun reflected, "but I believe that for this AI and technology boom, we are prepared. We have built more offices than anywhere else in the country."
Critics frequently warn that relying on tech liquidity creates a volatile, speculative housing market that could crash if tech stocks pull back. Toledano rebutted that today’s buyers put down 40% to 50% cash deposits compared to 5% to 10% in 2008, resulting in what he said is a 99.9% closing rate across 800 downtown Miami units he recently delivered.
"[In] the old days, in 2008, 2009, people used to put 5% or maybe 10% deposit, and this is why we saw that big crash. I don't think that this is happening in this cycle," he said.

"Florida cost of life has gone up, but so have incomes," Baboun noted. "Workforce housing [residents] are still making six figures. It's not like they're making $50,000 like they did 10 years back."

articles.title_orig: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
articles.title_zh: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
articles.content_orig:
State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors
California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.
Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: companies cannot mislead their investors.”
The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.
Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China .
Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.
Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.
“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”
Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.
Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, said the company had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back .
Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.
after newsletter promotion
Shares in rival chipmaker AMD closed down almost 8% on Thursday after the publication of reports connected to short seller Hunterbrook warning about its links to China and the “circular financing” of customers.
The company, which has been targeted amid the Nvidia scandal, is looking at a further fall of more than 5% in pre-market trading.
Hunterbrook Media published allegations on the use of AMD’s software by a Chinese server maker blacklisted by the US. Sister publication, The Bear Cave newsletter, alleged that AMD’s use of datacentre lease guarantees and backstops for unsold cloud computing capacity could leave it exposed to a pullback in AI spending.
AMD said the reports’ claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships”.
“AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” the company said. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.”
AMD’s share price has more than doubled so far this year, giving the company a market capitalisation of more than $800m.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine strains Russian logistics with Crimean bridge strikes
articles.title_zh: Ukraine strains Russian logistics with Crimean bridge strikes
articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin’s prized Kerch Bridge was struck for the third time this week early on Thursday, halting rail traffic between Russia and occupied Crimea just days after a section of the road bridge collapsed.
As its only direct link to the region, the bridge is strategically important as a military supply artery to Russia. It is also a powerful symbol of Russia’s continued control of Ukrainian territory – as Putin made its construction a key priority after Russia’s illegal annexation of the peninsula in 2014.
The third strike came at a significant moment, as Putin was about to meet US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Asia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described previous strikes on the bridge – conducted exclusively with Ukraine-made weapons – as being the seventh stage of what he called “an unprecedented operation in response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure.”
Some rail traffic across the bridge resumed on Thursday afternoon, according to Russia’s transport ministry, which said earlier there were no casualties.
Speaking to reporters in Shenzhen after the unprecedented trilateral meeting in China, Putin threatened Ukraine with “painful” retaliation for the attack. He claimed, despite ample evidence otherwise, that the bridge serves “purely peaceful purposes.”
Kyiv came under a renewed attack from Russian drones on Thursday afternoon. While many were shot down or disabled by Ukrainian air defenses, several got through and struck at the heart of the capital.
Two people were killed in the attack on Kyiv region and five others were injured in the Ukrainian capital, according to authorities.
Projectiles also struck near the embassies of the Netherlands and Austria in Kyiv, according to their governments . Though staff at both embassies were unharmed, the Dutch embassy sustained minor damage, the country’s foreign minister said.
The daytime assault came after Russia launched drone strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities, port infrastructure and vessels overnight. The Russian defense ministry said it hit two power substations in Odesa, a fuel storage facility in Chornomorsk and a cargo ship transporting goods to the port of Odesa. Russia also said it struck a power substation in the northeastern city of Sumy.
The latest attack on the bridge came as Putin was meeting Trump on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, ahead of their historic trilateral talks with Xi.
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Putin came out of the meeting in an “excellent mood,” adding that Ukraine was the main topic of discussion, Russian state news agency TASS reported.
Before the meeting, Trump praised his “great relationship” with Putin, calling him “my friend.”
Trump has renewed his push for a negotiated end to Russia’s war on Ukraine in recent months. He has at times been criticized by Kyiv and its European allies of adopting Russian narratives around the war.
Historic three-way talks between Trump, Xi and Putin underway
Meanwhile in Berlin, the so-called Coalition of the Willing – a group of Ukraine’s key allies – convened Thursday with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in attendance.
In a joint press briefing following the meeting, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz emphasized the group’s unwavering support for Kyiv, while British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that progress toward peace had “clearly” been made, adding that Europe “is ready to enter these negotiations.”
Also speaking during the briefing, Kushner said that Trump dialed into the coalition’s meeting and gave his assessment of his talks in Shenzhen. According to Kushner, he conveyed “a very strong message to both of them [Xi and Putin] on the desire for peace and would like to engage both of them very aggressively to get there.”
Zelensky, meanwhile, told reporters in Berlin that how long the war drags on would depend on “the readiness of the US to mediate and pressure (Russia).”
Referring to the trilateral in Shenzhen, Zelensky said both the US and China have the ability to help stop the war.
“If you want to stop Russia, stop trade between Russia and your country — China can do it. The United States can do it. And that’s it. Not enough for their (Russia’s) economy. Not enough for the war.”
The $3.7 billion Crimean Bridge was built to handle 40,000 cars a day and move 14 million passengers and 13 million tons of cargo per year, according to Russian state media.
Ukraine has targeted the Kerch Bridge repeatedly since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022, but the damage the bridge sustained this week appears to be more significant than in some of the previous attacks.
Ukraine has stepped up its attacks on Crimea in the past six months, forcing the Russian-installed authorities to impose a state of emergency over the summer because of widespread power outages and fuel shortages on the heavily militarized peninsula.
This story has been updated with additional developments.
CNN’s Nina Subkhanberdina, Anna Chernova, Victoria Butenko and Arina Porkhovnik contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Xi Jinping says a ‘full turnaround’ has been achieved in Australia-China relations, praising Anthony Albanese
articles.title_zh: Xi Jinping says a ‘full turnaround’ has been achieved in Australia-China relations, praising Anthony Albanese
articles.content_orig:
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake
Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.
Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump , California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway .
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.
“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.
Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep . Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.
Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News .
Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health , often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

articles.title_orig: Russia unleashes retaliatory barrage on Kyiv bridges
articles.title_zh: Russia unleashes retaliatory barrage on Kyiv bridges
articles.content_orig:
Russia launched a barrage of air attacks on Ukraine, killing eight people, as it targeted Kyiv’s bridges and infrastructure across the country.
The attacks overnight on Thursday into Friday hit vital transport bridges spanning the Dnipro River in the capital and knocked out power generation in several parts of Ukraine, officials said.
The missile and drone swarms came shortly after Russia’s President Vladimir Putin threatened retaliation for Ukraine’s targeting of a symbolic bridge linking his country with the Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow illegally annexed in 2014.
Eight ⁠people – including six in Kyiv – were killed in the overnight attacks, and ⁠28 wounded, ‌Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said in a social media post.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said ballistic missiles had damaged the Podilskyi, Darnitskyi, and Southern bridges, requiring traffic restrictions across the Dnipro.
Buildings, transport and logistics infrastructure were hit in several districts of the city, the Kyiv City Military Administration said in a statement. Citywide electricity disruptions were also reported.
Elsewhere, Ukrainian sources reported that one person was killed as a strike hit a hospital in the Zaporizhia region. Nuclear ⁠power plants across the country were forced to reduce operations, causing outages in Kyiv and 10 regions, First Deputy ‌Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said on Friday that road and rail bridges in Kyiv used to transport weapons and military equipment to ⁠the battlefield were targeted. It added that its forces hit defence ⁠industry facilities as well as energy and transport infrastructure in several regions of Ukraine.
The large-scale attack came hours after Putin pledged a “painful” response to Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch Bridge earlier this week. The attack severed the key road link across the Kerch Strait.
“We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that,” Putin told reporters on Thursday in China, where he attended a summit with the Chinese and United States presidents. Putin said the roadside of the bridge had been “seriously damaged” and pledged to rebuild it.
Ukraine continued its efforts to target energy and military infrastructure overnight. Russia’s Defence Ministry reported that its forces had intercepted 310 Ukrainian drones.
A Ukrainian drone ⁠attack damaged an ⁠industrial facility in Russia’s western ‌region of Smolensk, Governor Vasily Anokhin said on the ⁠Telegram messaging app, ⁠without identifying ⁠the facility.
The commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned ⁠Systems Forces said on Friday that 40 Russian oil ⁠facilities and defence ⁠industry targets have been hit over the past 50 days.
Moscow-installed officials in occupied eastern Ukraine also reported three people had been killed during an attack.
The overnight hostilities illustrate the lack of progress in US-led efforts to mediate a ceasefire.
US envoy Jared Kushner said on Thursday that Russia is comfortable with Europe joining the negotiations, and also with the idea of security guarantees for post-war Ukraine that are modelled on NATO’s Article 5, under which an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.
Early on Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said cooperation between Ukraine, the US and Europe on negotiations is “becoming closer” and that he hoped the US would organise the first multilateral meeting involving the Europeans “as soon as possible”.
Russian ⁠Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said ⁠later that ⁠a visit by three European Union representatives to Russia ‌is “under consideration”.
However, he added that any form of Ukrainian membership of NATO is unacceptable to Moscow.
“[E]ven the notion of a formula for Ukraine’s quasi-membership of NATO, and the search for some sort of – in inverted commas – ‘creative ⁠solution’ in this area, is an option that is ⁠unacceptable to us. We discuss security guarantees first and foremost in terms of ensuring the security of our own country,” Ryabkov was quoted as saying by the Interfax news agency.
“As far as Ukraine is concerned, let ⁠them recognise the irrevocable nature of our demand ⁠that this state must not join NATO. When that happens, I think the issue of security guarantees can be discussed in one way or another,” Ryabkov was quoted as adding.

articles.title_orig: Quantum Computing Is Even Weirder Than You Think
articles.title_zh: Quantum Computing Is Even Weirder Than You Think
articles.content_orig:
Shashwat Kumar and Rodrigo Cortiñas, Research Scientists, Google Quantum AI, Google Research
On a superconducting processor, we turned one of quantum mechanics’ strangest features into something you can measure, benchmark, and put to work across systems as large as 105 qubits.
Here is a Sunday paper-style puzzle you can try right now. Draw a 3×3 grid. Fill every cell with either +1 or −1, subject to two rules: each row must multiply to +1, and each column must multiply to −1.
You didn’t manage it, right? There is an elegant reason for that. For a row to multiply to +1, it needs an even number of −1s. For a column to multiply to −1, it needs an odd number. Add up the rows and you learn the grid contains an even number of −1s. Add up the columns and you learn it contains an odd number. Well…That’s impossible!
The grid would have to be two contradictory things at once. No such table exists; it is a paradox.
Now turn the puzzle into a game: Each round, Alice is handed a row and Bob a column. Without talking, Alice fills her row by the row rule and Bob fills his column by the column rule. They win if they put the same number in the square where their row and column intersect. Any plan made in advance is just a pre-written table, meaning at best they will win 8 out of 9 rounds. This changes if they use a quantum computer. It won't fill in the impossible grid, but in principle, it lets them win every round.
The reason is a property called quantum contextuality , arguably the strangest feature of quantum mechanics. Einstein once famously asked whether the moon is there when nobody looks, his way of insisting that physical properties ought to exist whether or not anyone measures them. For quantum systems, contextuality is the precise, experimentally testable statement that the answer can be no: you cannot assign fixed, pre-existing values to everything you might measure.
What a measurement yields can depend on which other compatible measurements you make alongside it (i.e., on its context ). This is not only a deep philosophical statement, but more so, cutting-edge science and the basis of a new technology. And in the game above, Alice and Bob can use it to engineer a solution. Their answers are not looked up in a hidden table written in advance; the table does not exist. Their answers come into being as they measure, and quantum correlations stitch them together more tightly than any classical rulebook permits.
Entanglement usually gets top billing as the “magic ingredient” of quantum computing. But a growing body of theory suggests contextuality is the deeper resource, the thing that actually powers certain quantum algorithms past their classical counterparts. The catch is that, until recently, contextuality had been demonstrated almost exclusively in small systems of a few particles. Whether it survives, and stays useful, in the many-body systems that real quantum computers are made of was an open question.
That is the question we set out to answer. In " Quantum-classical separation in bounded-resource tasks arising from measurement contextuality ," published in Science , we demonstrate and measure contextuality on our superconducting quantum processors. Our qubits win the magic square game 98.3% of the time, exceed the classical limit on a contextuality test, and outperform classical strategies in tasks spanning up to 105 qubits. Along the way, these tasks proved to be a sensitive new benchmark for quantum hardware, catching subtle errors that random-circuit tests miss.
We ran what is commonly called the magic square game on our Willow quantum processor. Alice and Bob each hold two qubits, sharing two entangled Bell pairs instead of a pre-written table, and measure them using preset settings for their assigned row or column to get their ±1 entries.
The best conceivable classical strategy loses at least one round in nine, winning at most 88.89% of the time. When we played all nine versions of the game 100,000 times apiece, our qubits lost roughly one in sixty, winning 98.30% of them (0.9830 ± 0.0001).
The gap is meaningful and statistically significant: our qubits coordinated better than any pre-written table allows. That's because no cell has a value fixed in advance. Each answer takes shape only when it is measured alongside the rest of its row or column (its context), and shared entanglement makes Alice's and Bob's answers for the shared cell agree.
With shared entanglement and a prearranged measurement plan, Alice and Bob can in principle agree at the intersection in every round. On our hardware, noise causes about one loss in 60.
The magic square game demonstrated the potential power of contextuality, so next we set out to measure how contextual a machine is. We used a Bell–Kochen–Specker inequality , closely related to the famous Bell test which showed that entangled particles like the Bell pairs above can't carry answers fixed in advance. Our inequality bundles a set of correlations into a single number, χ . In terms of the rows and columns from the game above it reads, χ = R1 + R2 + R3 − C1 − C2 − C3, where R and C represent the products of the rows and columns Alice and Bob had to calculate earlier:
Any universe where measurement outcomes are predetermined must obey χ ≤ 4 (try a few tables and you will see that χ can only take values -4, 0, and 4). Quantum mechanics permits values up to 6, which can only happen if all Rs = +1 and all Cs = -1. And unlike most such tests, this one is state-independent : it doesn’t matter how you prepare the qubits, which makes it a property of the machine rather than of a carefully chosen input.
Measuring χ is demanding: every row and column must be measured on the same two qubits, one after another, without disturbing them. We did this with an extra helper qubit (an "ancilla") that picks up each result and is measured instead, leaving the two main qubits intact. We ran 540 measurements in a row, repeated 1,000 times.
We measured χ = 5.590 ± 0.008.
Comfortably past the classical bound of 4 and only 7% away from the quantum limit. A number that says: the contextuality is in this machine in this quantity.
Two qubits are one thing, but quantum effects are fragile, and every added qubit brings noise that can wash them out. Useful quantum computing needs many qubits working together, so the question is whether contextuality survives at scale.
In the GHZ parity game , N players share one entangled GHZ state (a superposition of all qubits being 0 and all being 1). Each player gets a one-bit question and answers with one bit, without communicating. They win if the parity (even or odd) of all the answers matches a rule set by the questions. Random guessing wins half the time, and the best classical plan does only a bit better: 75% for three players, shrinking toward 50% as players are added. A shared GHZ state wins every time. We played with up to 71 players, one per qubit. Noise keeps us below 100% and grows with each added qubit, so our lead narrows, but we stay above the classical bound throughout. We also verified genuine entanglement across 45 qubits, more than the full size of many earlier GHZ experiments.
Each player measures their qubit in a basis set by their question bit. Despite hardware noise, the measured win rate stays above the best classical strategy by many standard deviations, up to 71 players.
Beyond multiplayer games, the same physics separates shallow quantum and classical circuits. In 2018, a landmark theorem proved that a specific problem, finding a hidden linear function , can be solved by a constant depth quantum circuit, and that no classical circuit of constant depth can. The source of this quantum advantage traces back to contextuality.
In this proof, constant depth matters. It means the circuit doesn’t get deeper as the problem gets bigger. Because every output bit is computed in a fixed number of steps, information has time to travel only a short distance. Each classical output can therefore o

Oops, something went wrong
The Anthropic ( ANT ) IPO hangover.
Shares of the model builder dropped 6% in premarket trading on Friday as investors booked profits after a frenetic first day of trading. Not helping sentiment: the broader market plunged on Anthropic's well-received IPO day and remains under pressure today.
Anthropic made a monster debut on Wall Street Thursday, with shares opening at $111.50 a little before noon ET, a 34% premium to the $83 IPO price.
But the AI company's stock couldn't hold on to its early gains.
The stock closed at $97.17, up 17% on the day.
That closing price gave Anthropic a market capitalization of about $1.28 trillion, or roughly $1.75 trillion on a fully diluted basis. Not bad for a company founded only five years ago, in a historic IPO that raised $81.3 billion.
"At a time in which investors are very nervous on the overall tech trade and the Nvidia black cloud moment casts a shadow over the tech sector, Anthropic's debut is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning," Yorkville Ives partner Dan Ives said.
Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Sozzi Unleashed morning show, the ' Power Players With Brian Sozzi' podcast and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team.

articles.title_orig: Putin scores ‘massive win’ at first trilateral meeting, rebuilding standing as Ukraine war grinds on
articles.title_zh: Putin scores ‘massive win’ at first trilateral meeting, rebuilding standing as Ukraine war grinds on
articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin came away from China stronger than he arrived, standing as an equal beside the leaders of the U.S. and China, both far more powerful than Russia, even as he remains bogged down in a war in Ukraine now in its fifth year.
Putin stood shoulder to shoulder with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping on a red-carpeted stage Thursday after the first-ever meeting between the three leaders. Trump publicly praised Putin as "my friend" as the two entered a separate bilateral meeting.
Putin was greeted at the APEC summit with smiles and handshakes, and he held bilateral meetings with at least seven world leaders over the two days. This came with the Ukraine war showing no signs of ending, more than four years after Russia invaded its neighbor.
"It's a massive win for Putin," said Joerg Wuttke, an expert at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group. It's "as if the world has forgiven."
Hours before the three-way meeting, Ukrainian forces struck the bridge linking Russia to Crimea, a peninsula annexed by Russia in 2014, for the third time this week. Russia retaliated with a major attack on Kyiv, killing several people and damaging Ukrainian infrastructure.
The two-day summit appeared to be a symbolic triumph, even as Moscow escalated the war and took a hard line during the European Union leaders' renewed push to end the conflict.
Despite few concrete outcomes, the first-ever three-way summit is "arguably a diplomatic victory for Moscow," said Andrius Tursa, an advisor for Central and Eastern Europe and Russia at Teneo. Putin will likely seek to institutionalize the format, Tursa said.
During the meeting and afterward, Putin and Trump railed against the International Criminal Court, which has had an arrest warrant out for Putin since March 2023. Trump called the court, which his administration has sanctioned, an out-of-control "rogue globalist organization." Putin said he would consider attending the December G20 meeting in Miami after discussing it with Trump.
The three leaders issued a joint declaration of peace after the trilateral talks. Beijing has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's aggression.
Putin later spent much of a press briefing after the trilateral meeting defending Moscow's decision to invade Ukraine, insisting that its root causes lie in NATO expansion and the alleged illegitimacy of Ukraine's leadership.
He also blamed the continued conflict on Ukraine's reluctance to accept terms. "If they truly want to end the conflict, they should agree to the compromises ... We accepted those terms; now, it is up to Ukraine."
This stance leaves "little scope for a ceasefire, let alone a durable settlement, absent a material shift in the military balance or political leadership in Moscow or Kyiv," Tursa said.
Russia lags both the U.S. and China in economic clout, population size, and most other major metrics of influence. Russian media, however, portrayed Putin's participation in discussions on global issues alongside the leaders of two major economic and military powers as a recognition of Russia's global power status and a setback for Western isolation efforts.
Putin said that all three leaders agreed that it's a "useful format," and such meetings could take place again.
"A key Kremlin objective will be to institutionalize such a great-power format," said Tursa. No concrete agreements on Ukraine were announced following the summit, and it remains unclear what, if anything, was settled with neither Kyiv nor European officials in the room.
One signal is whether the three leaders meet again in the near future, with the upcoming G20 summit in Miami a potential next opportunity, Tursa said.
Ukraine and European governments have said repeatedly that they must have a say in any talks on their security. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said ahead of the summit that big powers tend to assume they can decide the world's future, which he called a "huge mistake."

articles.title_orig: 4 British Men Convicted of Sexually Assaulting Joanne Young
articles.title_zh: 4 British Men Convicted of Sexually Assaulting Joanne Young
articles.content_orig:
The daughter of Joanne Young, who was drugged, raped and advertised for sex online by her husband, is among those calling for a change to the law on consent.
Philip Young drugged and abused his wife over a 13-year period , using websites and apps to invite men to their home in Swindon without her knowledge. On Thursday, four men were found guilty of sexual offences against her.
The trial has sparked calls for the government to ensure defendants cannot use "third-party consent" as a defence in rape trials of this nature.
Daughter Alex Young said: "It has been 23 years since this was last updated. Society has progressed, crime has progressed. So why hasn't the law progressed with it?"
Warning: This story discusses sexual violence and abuse
Philip Young advertised his wife for sex using websites such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers without her knowledge.
During the trial, the prosecution stated that the four men, who were all strangers to each other, failed to seek consent from Joanne Young before they engaged in sexual activity with her.
The defendants claimed they had been duped by Philip Young and believed she was consenting.
In a post on LinkedIn, Alex Young said: "We live in a world where there is debate over whether third-party consent is enough to have sex with someone.
"We live in a world where someone's partner can consent for them, and that is enough to use it as an argument in a court of law.
"This is simply unacceptable."
Her calls echo those made by her mother, who spoke on the steps of Winchester Crown Court after the trial.
"No-one should be able to give it [consent] on your behalf," said Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity.
"I urge the government to look at this as a priority so that women are properly protected in future."
The Sexual Offences Act 2003 states that "a person consents if he agrees by choice, and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice".
"If someone is drugged asleep and unconscious they can't give consent," Professor Miranda Horvath, director of the University of Suffolk's Institute for Social Justice and Crime, told the BBC.
"Someone can't give consent on your behalf.
"[Technology] is quickly evolving but we need to look at where improvements can be made in the legislation."
Like Joanne Young, Laura Bishop from Bristol has also waived her right to anonymity after her ex-husband received a 14-year prison sentence for drugging and raping her while inviting other men to abuse her.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme, Bishop said the crimes will affect her for the rest of her life.
"It's something that unfortunately you can never get over," she said.
"You have to try and remain positive and optimistic but the betrayal, particularly by men, is very difficult to move on from."
Bishop has a PhD in cyber crime and uses her expertise and experience to work with MPs and charities to improve governance around digital safety and regulations.
"The sites my husband used to advertise me are still active and are known by the police to not provide evidence and forensics when asked.
"So why are they still accessible?" she said.
Bishop understands why many choose to maintain their anonymity but wants to encourage those who can speak out to do so.
"There's a million reasons why its not be appropriate to waive your anonymity and it might just be because it's something you can't actively do," she said.
"But for those of us that are able to, we have to stand strong for victims."
Debbie Beadle, chief executive officer at Wiltshire-based domestic abuse charity Fear Free, also hopes that Joanne Young's decision to speak out will encourage others to do so.
"Six in seven rapes against women are done by someone they know and this adds a barrier to people coming forward," she said.
"The fact that Joanne has come forward will help us others when this has happened to them."
Horvath said more needed to be done to tackle and "de-platform" perpetrators.
"The research being conducted and the evidence base we have is emerging [because] these kinds of offences are under-reported and under-detected," she said.
"We need to ensure proper implementation of the legislation we have through suspect-focused investigation, prosecutions and resourcing and training of the professionals working in these environments.
"[We also need to be] holding the platforms and tech firms to account that are continuing to proliferate this material and saying 'this is enough, we will not tolerate this in our society'."
Prosecutors said Thursday's trial was the first of its kind in England, but former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, Jess Phillips, told LBC that she did not believe it would be the last unless changes were made.
"The ability of these men to find each other on websites that you and I could just log on to now just means that these cases are going to keep on coming," she said.
"The state needs to make sure that its online safety laws and regulations are strong enough to stop this from ever being able to happen," she said.
"I think that every single one of the websites listed in this case should be called on today to answer the questions, can you guarantee this isn't happening today?"
Phillips said there was "absolutely" a case for making it an offence to advertise another person for sex online and that exploitation of adults occurs "all across the internet" with "very little regulation on the safety or the certainty of consent".
The Domestic Abuse Commissioner, Dame Nicole Jacobs, has also called for the case to be a "turning point":
"Ultimately this case again highlights that we need to stop treating drug-facilitated sexual abuse as an isolated incident and recognise it for the form of horrific domestic abuse that it is," she said.

Anthropic fell nearly 6% on Friday morning after a historic debut on Nasdaq, as AI fears continued to cause a selloff with Nvidia and AMD lower.
The AI lab was 5.6% down in premarket trading at 4.23am ET on Friday.
Nvidia was down 1.66% and AMD fell 4.12%.
Anthropic soared 17% in its first day of trading on Thursday, after the company completed the biggest initial public offering on record, topping SpaceX' s historic debut in June. The stock closed at $97.17 per share.
Investors had hoped that Anthropic's debut would revitalize the AI trade, which has come under pressure in recent months amid fears over capex spending.
The sector has also had to contend with the fallout from Jensen Huang resigning as Nvidia CEO, alongside concerns that AI chip sales to Asia could slump as Washington cracks down on an export-control loophole.
On Thursday, short seller Hunterbrook Media alleged in a report that firmware sold by chipmaker AMD had turned up in U.S.-blacklisted companies. AMD stock closed down more than 7%. The chipmaker told CNBC it complies with U.S. law.
The House Foreign Affairs Committee also released documents showing that a subagency of the Commerce Department approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, highlighting a potential sales slowdown under stricter export controls.

articles.title_orig: ‘Dean Of Valuation’ Says Nvidia Is 30% Below Fair Value, Waits For $140 — Calls Jensen Huang ‘Great CEO, But Human’
articles.title_zh: ‘Dean Of Valuation’ Says Nvidia Is 30% Below Fair Value, Waits For $140 — Calls Jensen Huang ‘Great CEO, But Human’
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock rout after earnings refuses to let up.
Shares of the fallen AI chip darling are down more than 10% since the company's Nov. 17 earnings report. The stock is down 14% since founder Jensen Huang resigned on Nov. 12 under a cloud of controversy, notably over his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress made a pretty compelling case this week that Nvidia can keep running the AI money machine without Huang in the driver's seat.
The earnings numbers were enormous. The outlook was ahead of estimates. And Kress came across as a steady operator who knows this business inside and out.
Nvidia delivered $2.68 in adjusted earnings per share on $115.8 billion in revenue. Wall Street was looking for $2.47 and $109.15 billion.
The next-quarter forecast? Revenue of $127.4 billion to $132.6 billion. Again, comfortably ahead of expectations.
And Nvidia now sees fiscal 2028 revenue growth of 75%, up from the 70% forecast just three months ago. The AI spending machine is showing no signs of slowing down — at least, that's the story Kress pitched.
But here's where the story gets messy, and why the stock is likely getting drilled.
New Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones stumbled badly on the leadership question on the earnings call. Investors wanted urgency. They wanted a clear timeline for finding a permanent CEO. Instead, they got a message that left the door open to an extended interim arrangement.
That's a problem. Nvidia is the company at the center of the biggest technology boom in a generation. Wall Street doesn't want a leadership guessing game.
Kress proved she can handle the numbers. Jones still has to prove the board can handle succession to one of the most celebrated tech founders in decades. And right now, that may be Nvidia's biggest unanswered question.
"I don't know that any internal candidate, though, is capable of running the whole company," Seaport Research Partners analyst Jay Goldberg said on Sozzi Unleashed . "Jensen famously built the structure of the company around himself. Like he's the center of the wheel and all the things connect to him. And I don't think anyone internally has as complete a view of the company as Jensen does."
Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Sozzi Unleashed morning show, the ' Power Players With Brian Sozzi' podcast and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team.
